newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NZ rating not threatened by lower surplus - S&P.
newsitem.headline: NZ rating not threatened by lower surplus - S&P.

text.p: The recent weakening in New Zealand fiscal policy has no implications for the nation's credit rating, a top official with Standard & Poor's Corp said.
David Beers, managing director of S&P's sovereign rating division, said the coalition government's financial position is still strong despite the reduction in its forecast surpluses.
"We're not worried about a weakening in fiscal policy, which has been flagged to the marketplace for quite some time," Beers told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV) in an interview.
S&P early last year upgraded New Zealand's sovereign debt rating to AA+, a notch above Australia's AA rating.
The New Zealand government, in its budget last month, cut its forecast for its budget surplus in 1997/98 to NZ$1.5 billion from the earlier projection of NZ$3.3 billion.
The government cited lower-than-expected revenue growth and changes in welfare and debt servicing forecasts.
Beers said S&P had factored in this deterioration in fiscal policy when affirming New Zealand's rating after the formation of the centre-right coalition in December.
"The easing is still taking place against a background of great financial strength for the government. It's still running surpluses and paying down its debt," he said.
Beers said that while the budget position had deteriorated, this was still consistent with the present credit rating.
Beers was in Sydney as part of S&P's annual review of Australia's credit rating.
He is due to travel to New Zealand later this week.
